# Testing the generation of an `Innovation`

## Definition of epidemic parameters
In a population of fixed size, the \(\SIR\) epidemic runs under the following stochastic dynamics:
\begin{tabbing}
\emph{Xemovals:}\qquad\= The transition \(S\to S-1\), \;\= \((R \to R+1\) \= 
occurs at rate \(\beta \, I\), \kill
\emph{Infections:}    \> The transition \(S\to S-1\),   \> \(I \to I+1\)  \> 
occurs at rate \(\alpha \, S \, I\),\\
\emph{Removals:}      \> The transition \(I \to I-1\),  \> \(R \to R+1\)  \> 
occurs at rate \(\beta \, I\).     
\end{tabbing}
The structural parameter of epidemic `duration` 
(a positive real number)
and the `n₁` population size are given by
`julia` constants,
as are the per-pair infection rate `α` and the per-individual rate of removal `β`.
The population size is also given explicitly.
The variable `samplesize` holds the number of replicates of the simulation.
```{julia}
const duration = 2.0 
const α, β     = 0.2, 1.5 
const n₁       = 6  

samplesize = 10000 ;
```

## Simulation and storage of results
A sample of a random `Innovation` (with no conditional removals),
based on \(n\) time lines,
is generated using the following invocation:
`generate_innovation(n, duration, α=α, β=β)`.
Total numbers of `Infection`s with specified `infectee` marks
and numbers of `Removal`s with specified `target` marks are tabulated
in a `DataFrame` together with mean values.
The logic here is as follows:

(a) a given time line \(x+1\) accumulates (incoming) potential infections arising from contacts between
a `target` time line (lies strictly below time line \(x+1\))
and
an `infectee` time line (namely time line \(x+1\))
thus occurring at a rate \(α \, x(n-x)\), yielding specified infection rate;

(b) a given time line \(x\) accumulates potential removals arising from each of the time lines
\(x\) and lower,
thus removals for time line \(x\) must occur at a rate \(β\, x\), yielding specified removal rate.

The following function returns a `DataFrame` of time line identifiers, and
also counts
per time line of infections, removals
and differenced removals together with their expected numbers:

```{julia}
function simulate_innovations(n, t, α, β, samplesize)
  df = DataFrame() ;

  df[:, "Time line"]      = 1:n
  df.infections          .= 0 ;
  df[:, "E[infections]"]  = [α * (x - 1) * (n - x + 1) *  samplesize * t for x in 1:n] ;
  df.removals            .= 0 ;
  df[:, "E[removals]"]    = [β * x * samplesize * t for x in 1:n] ;
  
  for x in 1:samplesize
    iv = generate_innovation(n, t, α=α, β=β)
    df.infections += [length([z for z in iv.infections if z.infectee == i]) for i in 1:n]
    df.removals   += [length([z for z in iv.removals   if z.target   <= i]) for i in 1:n]
  end
  
  df[:, "Δremovals"]    = [df.removals[1];          diff(df.removals)]
  df[:, "E[Δremovals]"] = [df[:, "E[removals]"][1]; diff(df[:, "E[removals]"])]
  
  df[:, "p-val(I)"] = 
    2ccdf(Normal(), abs.(df.infections - df[:, "E[infections]"]) ./ .√(df[:, "E[infections]"]))
  df[:, "p-val(R)"] = 
    2ccdf(Normal(), abs.(df.removals - df[:, "E[removals]"]) ./ .√(df[:, "E[removals]"]))

return df
end ;
```
This simulation is invoked as follows, with the following result.
```{julia}
data = simulate_innovations(n₁, duration, α, β, samplesize);
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
Markdown.parse("Total population size is $n₁, simulation uses $samplesize replicates.")
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
header = [chop(sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), nn), head=1, tail=1) for nn in names(data)]
Markdown.parse(
pretty_table(String, data[:, header[2:end]]; header=header[2:end], alignment=[:r, :r, :r, :r, :r, :r, :l, :l],
formatters = (ft_printf("%5d",1:6), ft_round(2,7:8)), tf=tf_markdown)
)
```

## Statistical analysis
The `removals` column in `data` is cumulative over time lines, 
so independent data is obtained from `Δremovals`
together with `infections`.
Entries in both of `infections` and `Δremovals` are independent Poisson
with mean given by the corresponding `E[...]`. The 
normal approximation to the Poisson distribution applies here, allowing us to compute \(p\)-values
with ease.
```{julia}
function display_simulation_results(df)
  headers  = ["Time line", "infections", "E[infections]", "p-val(I)", 
                           "Δremovals",  "E[Δremovals]",  "p-val(R)"]
  Markdown.parse(
    pretty_table(String, df[:, headers], header=headers, tf=tf_markdown, 
      alignment=[:c, :r, :r, :l, :r, :r, :l],
      formatters = ((v, i, j)->(isnan(v) ? "---" : v),
        (v, i, j)->(v isa Real && j ∈ [4, 7] && v<0.015 ? "** **$(round(v, digits=2))**" : v),
        (v, i, j)->(v isa Real && j ∈ [4, 7] && v<0.055 ? "* *$(round(v, digits=2))*" : v),
        (v, i, j)->(v isa Real && j ∈ [4, 7]            ? "$(round(v, digits=2))" : v),
        ft_printf("%4.2f", [4,7])),
  ))
end ;
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
Markdown.parse("Total population size is $n₁, simulation uses $samplesize replicates:")
```
```{julia}
#| echo: false
display_simulation_results(data)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Assessment
In a sequence of \(11\) independent \(Z\)-tests, no \(p\)-values are at \(0.01\) level or lower.
:::

## An example using a larger population.
This repeats the simulations of the previous section for a larger population.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
const n₂ = 11 
data = simulate_innovations(n₂, duration, α, β, samplesize) 

Markdown.parse("Total population size is $n₂, simulation uses $samplesize replicates:")
```
```{julia}
display_simulation_results(data)
```
::: {.callout-tip}
## Assessment
In a sequence of \(21\) independent \(Z\)-tests there is just one \(p\)-value at \(0.01\) level or lower.
:::

\newpage

## An example using a still larger population.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
const n₃ = 16 
data = simulate_innovations(n₃, duration, α, β, samplesize) 

Markdown.parse("Total population size is $n₃, simulation uses $samplesize replicates:")
```
```{julia}
#| echo: false
display_simulation_results(data)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Assessment
In a sequence of \(31\) independent \(Z\)-tests there are no \(p\)-values at the edge of \(0.01\) level.
:::


\newpage

## An example using a yet larger population.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
const n₄   = 24 
samplesize = 4samplesize
data = simulate_innovations(n₄, duration, α, β, samplesize) 

Markdown.parse("Total population size is $n₄, simulation uses $samplesize replicates:")
```
```{julia}
#| echo: false
display_simulation_results(data)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Assessment
In a sequence of \(63\) independent \(Z\)-tests, only one of the \(p\)-values is around or below level \(0.05\).
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
## Overall assessment
In a total of \(110\) independent \(Z\)-tests, one of the \(p\)-values is around or below level \(0.01\),
and one other is around or below level \(0.05\).
:::
